behavior_items: The reproducer is a Fortran 90 source file that successfully compiled with a 2025-06-03 GCC 16 snapshot but fails with a 2025-06-05 GCC 16 snapshot, so it exercises a regression introduced between those revisions rather than a long-standing front-end rejection of the source program.

Compilation stops while entering or lowering `SUBROUTINE get_c_attr(attrname, attrval_c)`, reported at source line 177, which means the problematic construct is reached during semantic lowering / gimplification of that procedure rather than during later optimization or final code generation.

The failing internal expression shown by gfortran is `_17 = D.6220 + 18446744073709551615;`. The constant `18446744073709551615` is `2^64 - 1`, the all-bits-set value for a 64-bit unsigned type, and is also the canonical unsigned representation of `-1` after wraparound.

The diagnostic explicitly says `type mismatch in binary expression` and then prints the participating types as `unsigned long`, `integer(kind=8)`, and `unsigned long`. This shows that one operand is represented in GCC internals as an unsigned host / target integer type while another operand is still a Fortran signed 8-byte integer node, and the gimplifier or verifier now refuses to combine them in one arithmetic expression.

Because the bad operation is addition by the unsigned all-ones constant, the reproducer likely triggers compiler-generated index, bound, length, offset, or descriptor arithmetic that conceptually subtracts one from a value. Instead of preserving a signed Fortran `integer(kind=8)` `-1`, the compiler materializes the adjustment as an `unsigned long` literal and then tries to add it to a signed `integer(kind=8)` temporary.

That pattern is typical of front-end generated bookkeeping for arrays, character lengths, descriptors, or attribute lookup tables inside a subroutine body. The user code does not need to contain a literal `18446744073709551615`; the reproducer mainly exercises a source construct that causes gfortran to synthesize such an offset expression during lowering.

The name `get_c_attr` suggests the procedure likely interacts with C-oriented metadata, descriptors, or character attribute handling. Such code paths commonly mix GCC size / byte-count types (`size_t`, `unsigned long`, pointer offsets) with Fortran scalar integer kinds, making them sensitive to signedness mistakes introduced by recent changes.

The regression message in the bug title mentions an ICE in `verify_gimple_in_seq`, and the current output shows a front-end error instead of a crash. Together, that indicates the underlying issue is malformed GIMPLE being built for this procedure: an earlier compiler snapshot probably either accepted the mixed-type tree or had not yet added the stricter verification, while the regressing snapshot detects the invalid typed binary operation earlier and emits an error instead of proceeding.

The compiler behavior exercised here is therefore not ordinary user-level type checking of a Fortran expression. It is validation of an internal compiler-generated expression whose operands should have been converted to a common type before gimplification. The reproducer demonstrates that some lowering path forgot to insert the necessary conversion from `integer(kind=8)` to the unsigned type, or vice versa.

The fact that the failing snapshots are built with ASan/UBSan is probably incidental; the important observable behavior is deterministic compile-time failure on a specific front-end lowering path. Sanitizers may only make the regression easier to catch during testing, but the emitted type-mismatch diagnostic already identifies the essential bug as incorrect internal type construction.

Wrap a SAVE_EXPR around EXPR, if appropriate. Do this to any expression which may be used in more than one place, but must be evaluated only once. Normally, expand_expr would reevaluate the expression each time. Calling save_expr produces something that is evaluated and recorded the first time expand_expr is called on it. Subsequent calls to expand_expr just reuse the recorded value. The call to expand_expr that generates code that actually computes the value is the first call *at compile time*. Subsequent calls at compile time* generate code to use the saved value. This produces correct result provided that *at run time* control always flows through the insns made by the first expand_expr before reaching the other places where the save_expr was evaluated. You, the caller of save_expr, must make sure this is so. Constants, and certain read-only nodes, are returned with no SAVE_EXPR because that is safe. Subroutine of stabilize_reference; this is called for subtrees of references. Any expression with side-effects must be put in a SAVE_EXPR to ensure that it is only evaluated once. We don't put SAVE_EXPR nodes around everything, because assigning very simple expressions to temporaries causes us to miss good opportunities for optimizations. Among other things, the opportunity to fold in the addition of a constant into an addressing mode often gets lost, e.g. "y[i+1] += x;". We can get declarations that are not possible to reference for various reasons: 1) When analyzing C++ virtual tables. C++ virtual tables do have known constructors even when they are keyed to other compilation unit. Those tables can contain pointers to methods and vars in other units. Those methods have both STATIC and EXTERNAL set. 2) In WHOPR mode devirtualization might lead to reference to method that was partitioned elsehwere. In this case we have static VAR_DECL or FUNCTION_DECL that has no corresponding callgraph/varpool node declaring the body. 3) COMDAT functions referred by external vtables that we devirtualize only during final compilation stage. At this time we already decided that we will not output the function body and thus we can't reference the symbol directly.

gcc/gimple-fold.cc.summary: Simplify a call to the strcat builtin. DST and SRC are the arguments to the call. Return NULL_TREE if no simplification was possible, otherwise return the simplified form of the call as a tree. The simplified form may be a constant or other expression which computes the same value, but in a more efficient manner (including calls to other builtin functions). The call may contain arguments which need to be evaluated, but which are not useful to determine the result of the call. In this case we return a chain of COMPOUND_EXPRs. The LHS of each COMPOUND_EXPR will be an argument which must be evaluated. COMPOUND_EXPRs are chained through their RHS. The RHS of the last COMPOUND_EXPR in the chain will contain the tree for the simplified form of the builtin function call.

reviewed_methods.summary: Return true if the conversion from INNER_TYPE to OUTER_TYPE is a useless type conversion, otherwise return false. This function implicitly defines the middle-end type system. With the notion of 'a < b' meaning that useless_type_conversion_p (a, b) holds and 'a > b' meaning that useless_type_conversion_p (b, a) holds, the following invariants shall be fulfilled: 1) useless_type_conversion_p is transitive. If a < b and b < c then a < c. 2) useless_type_conversion_p is not symmetric. From a < b does not follow a > b. 3) Types define the available set of operations applicable to values. A type conversion is useless if the operations for the target type is a subset of the operations for the source type. For example casts to void* are useless, casts from void* are not (void* can't be dereferenced or offsetted, but copied, hence its set of operations is a strict subset of that of all other data pointer types). Casts to const T* are useless (can't be written to), casts from const T* to T* are not.
